paper_title: RoomTokens: Masked Diffusion over Structured Tokens for Indoor Scene Synthesis

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generating 3D indoor scenes requires a representation that captures object semantics, instance identity, height structure, and orientation while respecting room geometry. Methods that model scenes as sequences of object vectors learn spatial constraints implicitly, leaving collisions and boundary violations to losses or post-processing; semantic-map methods make occupancy explicit, but collapse instance and directional structure. We introduce RoomTokens, a sliced structured-token representation in which each token stores semantic class, instance-color identity, and facing field. This representation allows a scene to be generated as a discrete grid while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), a masked discrete diffusion model that denoises semantic/instance-color/facing channels jointly with a shared cross-slice backbone. Architectural tokens are clamped as explicit floor- plan constraints, so the model samples furniture layouts that respect room geometry while retaining instance and object-attribute structure. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that RoomTokens with MDIRT improve layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods, suggesting structured spatial tokens as a practical choice for discrete 3D scene synthesis.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Automatic generation of 3D scenes is increasingly important, as it allows for scaling up of training data for 3D scene understanding and embodied AI, and provides content for applications such as augmented reality, gaming, and entertainment. Compositional 3D indoor scene generation (Tam et al., 2026b) formulates the problem as an object arrangement problem, where we must decide on object categories, individual object identities, placement, and orientation while respecting the geometry of the room. To ensure that generated scenes are plausible, it is important to model the spatial structure and object-level semantics together. Most existing methods represent scenes as sets or sequences of object vectors (Paschalidou et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026; Lin and Mu, 2024), where each object vector encodes the object category and bounding box of the object. While this representation is compact, it does not make occupancy constraints explicit and cannot ensure that two generated boxes do not occupy the same space. As result, generated scenes may contain inter-object collisions, wall penetrations, and inadequate clearance for accessing objects and room regions. Prior systems therefore add auxiliary mechanisms, such as intersection penalties in the training objective (Tang et al., 2024), rejectionstyle resampling of invalid insertions (Ritchie et al., 2019), or optimization-based layout refinement after an initial prediction (Luo et al., 2020). Another line of work (Feng et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026) leverages the broad knowledge encoded in LLMs/VLMs for more extensive semantic priors, but their coordinate outputs still require geometric cleanup and potentially multiple passes with visual critic to ensure physically plausible scene. Approaches that generate scenes based on semantic-maps (Yang et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2026) capture the spatial arrangements explicitly by assigning semantic labels to cells on dense grid. recent work, SemLayoutDiff (Sun et al., 2026) demonstrated improved floor-plan-conditioned generation with fewer collisions and out-of-boundary objects. However, single top-down semantic 1 Figure 1: Top. Comparison of scene representations for indoor scene generation. Object sequences (a) encode object attributes but lack explicit spatial relationship information. Semantic maps (b) make spatial structure explicit, but lack vertical, instance, and orientation information. We propose RoomTokens (c) to address these missing factors by encoding semantic occupancy, instance identity, and facing cues in sliced spatial grid. Bottom. We introduce MDIRT (d), masked discrete diffusion model over RoomTokens, which denoises missing token fields while keeping architectural tokens fixed so generated scenes respect room boundaries. map fails to capture important information needed for 3D scene generation. It collapses vertical information, merges adjacent objects of the same category under connected-component decoding, and provides no directional cue for estimating object orientation. In this work, we tackle the challenge of how to introduce instance-level and vertical information into these spatial maps. We introduce RoomTokens, sliced structured-token representation for indoor scenes. We represent room as stack of height-aware grids, with each grid cell storing RoomToken with three fields that capture the semantic class, the instance identity, and facing cues. Encoding the instance identity is challenging as the assignment of particular ID to an object is arbitrary (i.e., can be permuted or re-assigned), and the number of objects in scene is not fixed. As our aim is to distinguish spatially adjacent object instances on planar map (vs. providing an instance ID), we can use four colors (following the four-color theorem (Robertson et al., 1997)) to identify different instances. For orientation, the facing field encodes whether furniture token occupies the body or front half of an object; non-furniture tokens use none. We find that these two furniture labels are sufficient for decoding orientation. Together, these properties provide sufficient information for model to generate discrete spatial layout while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), single-stage masked discrete diffusion model for indoor scene generation. Each token property is embedded as semantic, instance-color, or facing channel. The channels are processed by shared cross-slice UNet and decoded jointly. The denoising process maps masked RoomTokens to structured 3D scene layouts while conditioning on and clamping the architectural tokens from the floor plan (Fig. 1 (bottom)), so furniture tokens are generated within the valid interior region defined by the architectural condition. Instead of predicting semantics and then instance-level attributes as in prior work (Sun et al., 2026), this multichannel parameterization learns semantic, instancecolor, and facing dependencies through shared features in single reverse process. Experiments on 3D-FRONT (Fu et al., 2021a) show that MDIRT generates more plausible layouts compared with SEMLAYOUTDIFF (Sun et al., 2026). Generated layouts better match reference rooms (FID 50.14 vs. 71.18) and capture more plausible object relations (Pair-Rel 12.09 vs. 20.65). They also contain fewer collisions (COL 12.64 vs. 16.24) and leave doors and windows more unobstructed (OC 82.31 vs. 56.02). In summary, our contributions are: 1) sliced structured RoomToken representation that stores semantic class, graph-color instance identity, and facing information in each height-aware grid token. 2) single-stage masked discrete diffusion model, MDIRT, for RoomTokens that clamps the architectural condition throughout denoising so furniture is generated within the valid room 2 interior, while jointly modeling semantic/instance-color/facing channels with shared cross-slice backbone. 3) An empirical analysis showing that explicit instance-color and facing fields improve instance recovery and orientation estimation and provide for physically plausible scene layouts.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Object-vector and relational scene synthesis. Many indoor scene synthesis methods represent room as set or sequence of objects with attributes specifying the semantic class, position, and orientation of objects. Early neural and graph-based approaches learn spatial priors over object arrangements (Wang et al., 2018; Ritchie et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020), while recent autoregressive and diffusion methods predict the object attributes directly (Wang et al., 2021; Paschalidou et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2024b; Tang et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026; Maillard et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025b). Other recent work leverages scene graphs, relational triples, or mixed graph diffusion for improved modeling of object layouts (Lin and Mu, 2024; Zhai et al., 2023; 2024; Bai et al., 2025; Ruiz et al., 2025), and physical or human-aware constraint objectives and optimization (Yi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024a; Sun et al., 2024a; Su et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026). These methods differ in conditioning and priors, but their generated layout is ultimately set of object bounding boxes. As result, generated scenes may contain object collisions and boundary overlaps, and additional post-processing is required as the representation does not natively prevent these. MDIRT instead generates discrete occupancy grid, where each cell has single semantic assignment and grid-level overlap is therefore explicit. By modeling object occupancy explicitly across height-aware slices, the representation helps reduce inter-object collisions. LLM and agent-based scene generation. By leveraging LLMs and VLMs, it is possible to condition on language input and access the common sense knowledge of how objects are positioned, stored in these pretrained models. LayoutGPT (Feng et al., 2023) predicts layouts with language models, while Holodeck (Yang et al., 2024b), AnyHome (Wen et al., 2024), SceneTeller ( Ocal et al., 2024), and open-universe systems (Aguina-Kang et al., 2024) connect text prompts with object retrieval, constraint solving, or scene assembly. More recent LLM/VLM and agentic methods use program synthesis, visual-language feedback, or multi-agent refinement for broader controllability (Hu et al., 2024; elen et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025; Pfaff et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2025). These systems provide flexible interfaces, but coordinateor program-level outputs still require geometric cleanup for dense indoor layouts. Our focus is complementary: we learn the layout distribution from annotated 3D-FRONT rooms and make the representation itself carry local occupancy, instance, and orientation structure. Discrete spatial representations for scene synthesis. Discrete spatial representations encode the scene by assigning labels directly to locations on 2D or 3D lattice, making occupancy constraints local and explicit. Yang et al. (2021) use voxel labels, Lee et al. (2023) model scene-scale categorical 3D data, and SemLayoutDiff (Sun et al., 2026) applies multinomial discrete diffusion to top-down semantic map. This family is closest to ours because it moves generation from unordered boxes toward explicit spatial fields. However, semantic-only spatial grids do not distinguish touching same-class instances, top-down maps collapse vertical structure, and single class label per cell provides no direct orientation cue. Our representation keeps the grid advantage but upgrades each sliced cell into structured RoomToken carrying semantic, instance-color, and facing fields. Graph coloring is used to assign instance colors during preprocessing, with the four-color theorem (Appel and Haken, 1977; Robertson et al., 1997) providing the minimum number of colors needed for separating adjacent same-class instances. Similar coloring ideas have been studied for discriminative instance segmentation (Kulikov et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2025), but remain largely unexplored as compact instance channels for generative modelling. Discrete diffusion and masked token modeling. Masked discrete diffusion corrupts categorical data by replacing tokens with absorbing mask states and trains denoiser to reverse that process. Multinomial and masked variants (Hoogeboom et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2024; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025) have become effective for discrete sequences and token grids. Layoutspecific diffusion models also use discrete or mixed discrete-continuous variables for structured 2D layouts and indoor scene attributes (Chai et al., 2023; Inoue et al., 2023; Levi et al., 2023; Hui et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2026), but these variables are often organized as layout tokens or object attributes rather than as per-cell scene occupancy fields. We extend masked discrete diffusion from 3 Figure 2: RoomToken data representation. (a) 3D scene is represented as horizontal slices taken at selected vertical heights. (b) Each slice encodes three aligned 2D channels: semantic class, instance-color identity, and the facing field. Stacking these channels over all heights forms sliced token volume. (c) The resulting 3D representation of stacked slices (RoomTokens) stores semantic, instance, and orientation information, with height derived from the slice index. Figure 3: Overview of MDIRT. Given selected height slices and an architectural mask, we clamp the fixed room structure and denoise masked interior RoomTokens with shared UNet with cross-slice attention. The denoiser predicts semantic, instance-color, and facing slices under semantic-gated validity constraints: architecture/background tokens carry no instance-color or facing cues, while furniture tokens do. The valid RoomToken grid is then grouped into object records, whose category, size, and pose are used to retrieve and place matched 3D assets. single semantic map or object-attribute tokenization to structured RoomTokens. MDIRT uses multichannel parameterization for training, where semantic, instance-color, and facing values are denoised together under validity constraints and floor-plan conditioning.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: Given room type and an input architectural mask (arch mask), MDIRT generates complete object-level 3D layout  (Fig. 3)  . With our RoomToken representation, slices at different heights store semantic occupancy with instance and facing cues, allowing objects to be recovered from the grid tokens (Sec. 3.1). We use masked diffusion to generate interior RoomTokens while keeping the architectural tokens fixed (Sec. 3.2). At each reverse step, multichannel denoising network gθ predicts the masked fields across height slices (Sec. 3.3). Finally, during scene assembly, the token grid is converted into object records and matching assets are retrieved for the final scene (Sec. 3.4). 3.1 SLICED ROOMTOKENS To recover object instances and poses from discrete occupancy map, we encode each room as stack of sliced RoomTokens. We discretize the floor plane into an grid and use selected height slices = {ζ1, . . . , ζS} to capture the vertical extent  (Fig. 2)  . We choose these heights by greedy coverage over furniture height intervals in the training set: each object covers candidate height if its vertical interval intersects [h τ, + τ ], with τ =0.10m matching the rasterization tolerance. Starting from fixed floor and ceiling anchors, we repeatedly add the candidate height that covers the most previously uncovered objects. We provide the specific grid size, slice heights, and other parameters in Sec. 4.1. 4 We index token by = (u, v, s), where {1, . . . , H}, {1, . . . , }, and {1, . . . , S}. The instance-color label is either one of instance colors or the none value c; the facing label is body, front, or the none value . The three values must agree with the semantic class. This projection removes only invalid semanticattribute combinations; it does not merge instances or change placement. We analyze the token validity before and after projection during denoising in App. B. During denoising, within each reverse step, semantic labels are updated first, then instance-color and facing predictions are recomputed from the updated semantic state. Labels that are already revealed are retained. If the semantic label is masked, both instance-color and facing attributes remain masked. When architecture/background is revealed, the attributes are set to null. To summarize, mask value denotes an unknown value, whereas null denotes an inapplicable attribute. This semantic-priority sampling occurs within one reverse process. See App. for details.

sections.title: 3.3 MULTICHANNEL DENOISING NETWORK
sections.content: We train multichannel denoising network gθ to predict label probabilities for masked out tokens. The model gθ consists of shared UNet Uθ which processes the summed field embeddings across height slices, and three prediction heads (Dy, Dc, Df ) for the semantic, instance-color, and facing fields. At each cell i, the three output heads produce the logits ℓy that define the label probabilities used in Sec. 3.2. , ℓf , ℓc Joint RoomToken denoising. The main denoising step predicts the RoomToken values from single shared hidden representation hθ, conditioned on the room type and arch mask a. For channel embeddings Ey, Ec, Ef , shared UNet Uθ, and output heads Dy, Dc, Df , the embedding token et,i at position for the denoised map at time is given by: et,i = Ey(zy t,i) + Ec(zc hθ = Uθ(et; t, κ), t,i) + Ef (zf t,i), ℓρ = Dρ(hθ,i), for each grid location i, ρ {y, c, }. (4) Here hθ,i is the hidden feature, ℓρ the logits for channel ρ, and κ = (r, a) the conditioning input. The clean xi and noisy zt,i variables are discrete categorical states; et,i and hθ,i are continuous vectors, and the three decoders map the shared vector to categorical channel logits. Summed embeddings and shared hidden state parameterize one RoomToken distribution rather than semantic-then-attribute pipeline. Cross-slice consistency. Cross-slice attention provides information exchange across height slices at the same floor location. The UNet treats the grid as the spatial domain after concatenating slice embeddings per location. At attention resolutions, cross-slice block reshapes each (u, v) feature into tokens, applies attention along the slice dimension, and writes the result back through residual projection. Thus, predictions for {(u, v, s) : = 1, . . . , S} exchange evidence about object extent and body/front alignment. Cross-channel consistency. Cross-channel consistency makes instance-color and facing predictions depend on the semantic prediction. Instance-color and facing logits share the semantic backbone features, and the attribute branch is modulated by semantic feature branch through learned gates and biases. This makes attributes semantic-aware within the same denoising step, while Sec. 3.2 enforces channel combinations are valid during sampling. Training objective. The training objective supervises both token denoising and the geometric quantities needed for scene assembly. The main terms denoise the masked RoomToken channels, while auxiliary terms calibrate occupancy and the geometric heads used downstream. We optimize = λyLy + λclsLcls + λcLc + λf Lf + λoccLocc + λattrLattr. (5) Here, each λ is scalar weight. Ly is masked cross-entropy over semantic classes, while Lcls is an object-count-balanced semantic class loss for the long-tailed furniture distribution. It applies fixed inverse-square-root weights computed from training object counts, keeps architecture/background weights at one, averages semantic cross-entropy over the cells of each ground-truth object, and then averages over objects. This gives rare categories and small instances comparable influence to common or large furniture. Lc and Lf are masked cross-entropy losses for instance-color and facing labels on visible furniture cells. Locc is binary cross-entropy with logits on foreground occupancy derived from the semantic logits. Lattr groups instance-level mean-squared regression losses for yaw (cos θ, sin θ), height, and vertical offset from instance-pooled features. See Sec. D.2 for details. 3. INFERENCE AND SCENE ASSEMBLY At inference, architectural cells from the input arch mask are clamped throughout the reverse process, and MDIRT samples semantic, instance-color, and facing slices for the furnished interior. Because these architectural tokens are never overwritten, the masked discrete diffusion design preserves the architectural condition throughout generation, enabling the model to learn furniture layouts within the valid room interior. In our experiments (Sec. 4.2), we show that there are zero out-of-bounds errors after final asset placement. We group connected RoomTokens with the same semantic and instance-color labels into object instances. Their tokens determine category, horizontal center, and horizontal dimensions; body/front 6 labels indicate orientation. MLP heads within MDIRT use denoising features averaged over each instance mask to predict continuous height and vertical offset, with yaw head providing orientation when body/front labels do not determine it. We instantiate the final scene by retrieving appropriate 3D assets from 3D-FUTURE (Fu et al., 2021b). For each object, we query the 3D database with the object category and select the closest asset based on the 3D extents. The retrieved asset is scaled along each axis to match the estimated extents, rotated to the predicted yaw, and translated to the recovered object position. We use the same categoryand size-based asset retrieval and placement process as SemLayoutDiff. After asset placement, there is no clipping, extra optimization, or any hand-designed scene correction. App. details assembly and the grouping/orientation procedures for the field-removal ablations.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate architecture-conditioned generation against recent diffusion methods. Ablations and user study assess design choices and perceived quality. 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Dataset. We train and evaluate on 3D-FRONT (Fu et al., 2021a) following splits established in prior work (Paschalidou et al., 2021) with 4,496 train / 274 val / 390 test rooms over three room types (bedroom, living room, and dining room). Model details. Following SemLayoutDiff (Sun et al., 2026), we train all methods as single unified model across room types rather than one model per room type. Each scene is rasterized on 128128 floor-plane grid, where one pixel/token has side length 0.10 in the horizontal plane. The grid is repeated over S=8 fixed height slices at (0.02, 0.45, 0.80, 1.20, 1.60, 2.00, 2.40, 2.70) m, which are selected once by greedy coverage analysis with 0.10 vertical tolerance. For MDIRT, RoomTokens use Ksem=39 semantic classes, C=3 instance colors plus c, and body/front/f facing labels; valid semanticinstance-colorfacing triples are flattened into 209-id palette for visualizations and the single-channel ablation. See Sec. D.1 for model details and App. for data processing details. Baselines. We compare DIFFUSCENE (Tang et al., 2024) (continuous diffusion), MIDIFFUSION (Hu et al., 2026) (mixed discrete-continuous diffusion), and SEMLAYOUTDIFF (Sun et al., 2026) (semantic-map diffusion), all trained as unified models on the same 3D-FRONT split. We also retrain SEMLAYOUTDIFF variant that retains multinomial diffusion while fixing exterior, door, and window pixels during training and sampling, restricting furniture to valid floor regions. We follow SemLayoutDiffs generation and evaluation procedures and reproduce their reported results for baselines. Metrics. Following prior work (Sun et al., 2026), we use FID and KID to assess rendered layout fidelity and CKL to compare object-category distributions against the 3D-FRONT test set. We introduce Pair-Rel to compare object-pair categories and spatial relations. For physical plausibility, we report out-of-boundary rates for scenes (OOBS) and objects (OOBO), object collisions (COL), navigability (NAV), and our door/window opening-clearance metric (OC). We also report the mean number of objects per scene (#Obj.). Metric definitions and computation details are in App. A. All scene-quality metrics are computed after asset retrieval, scaling, rotation, and placement, using the same 3D-FUTURE assets, SceneToolkit rendering, and evaluation scripts as SemLayoutDiff. No subsequent clipping, optimization, or hand-designed scene correction is applied. 4.2 RESULTS AND ANALYSIS Physical validity with competitive layout quality. We therefore also assess object relations, physical plausibility, and human preference. SemLayoutDiff with architecture clamping reduces OOB but raises COL from 16.24 to 40.89 because its reverse process denoises random semantic values rather than masked furniture under fixed architecture. Clamping also cannot account for geometry added during grouping, retrieval, and rotation, so some objects remain partially outside the room. By jointly modeling arch-conditioned semantic, instance-color, and facing slices, MDIRT achieves zero OOB while retaining low collision with small variation in COL and OC across runs. MDIRT reduces visible layout failures. Figure 4 shows that the quantitative improvements are visible in the generated layouts: baseline methods can place objects across boundaries, collide nearby furniture, or block architectural openings such as doors and windows, while MDIRT better preserves clear openings, room geometry, and object structure. See App. for additional results. ABLATION AND FAILURE ANALYSIS. We conduct ablation experiments on our model to determine the impact of different components (Tabs. 2 and 3). All ablation models are trained from scratch with the same data split and training settings, changing only the specified component. All use the architectural condition and the same scene assembly, rendering, and evaluation procedure. Class balancing and multichannel prediction. Without class balancing (Lcls), object count falls from 8.36 to 6.31 and CKL rises from 6.43 to 21.31, yielding sparser scenes with less accurate category frequencies. Combining the three fields into one categorical token, with all eight slices retained, raises FID from 49.84 to 95.35 and Pair-Rel from 12.13 to 48.32, supporting multichannel prediction. Instance color and facing. Removing the instance-color field raises COL to 88.77, indicating less reliable separation of object instances. Removing the facing field raises COL to 89.07 and lowers NAV from 99.30 to 75.69, indicating more overlap and less navigable scenes. Without instance color, connected same-category tokens form one instance. Without facing, an auxiliary head predicts the orientation from instance features (App. F). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: implausible layouts (green), object intersections (orange), and blocked We presented MDIRT, masked discrete diffusion framework over sliced RoomTokens for indoor scene layouts. RoomTokens add height slices, instance-color cues, and facing cues to semantic occupancy maps. Clamping architectural tokens during denoising preserves the supplied floor plan, keeping room geometry explicit while supporting object grouping, orientation estimation, and scene assembly. On 3D-FRONT, MDIRT achieves competitive distribution quality and the strongest overall spatial plausibility among evaluated methods. Controlled comparisons show gains beyond architecture 10 clamping and sparse generation; blinded human ranking study favors our scenes. Representation checks show little information loss; ablations support factorized RoomToken fields, semanticpriority sampling, and cross-slice attention. Structured occupancy tokens could also support outdoor scenes, objects with parts, and other semantic occupancy tasks. Limitations. The fixed grid and height slices can miss fine details and narrow gaps. The small 3D-FRONT training set is uneven across object categories and room types. RoomTokens and validity projection cannot prevent mesh collisions from grouping, continuous pose estimation, scaling, or asset retrieval. Larger, more diverse data and stronger scene assembly could improve distribution matching and retrieval; adaptive-resolution slices and geometry-aware refinement could capture details and reduce collisions.

sections.title: A EVALUATION METRICS
sections.content: We follow prior work (Sun et al., 2026) and evaluate the distribution similarity of generated scenes to reference scenes, as well as physical layout plausibility with metrics introduced in SceneEval (Tam et al., 2026a). Distribution and semantic quality. For FID and KID, we render each generated scene and each 3DFRONT test scene as 256256 orthographic top-down image. Objects are colored by semantic category, using the same fixed room-type palette for generated and test scenes. We convert the renders to RGB and white-pad them to 256256. We extract clean-fid clean Inception features and compute FID and KID from these features. For each comparison, we use equal-sized image sets, sample without replacement from the larger set, and average scores over ten draws. The aggregate MDIRT score compares all 390 test renders with 390 renders drawn from 3,000 generated scenes on each draw; per-room scores are computed separately. KID is reported multiplied by 103. CKL is DKL(pgtpgen) between normalized furniture-category counts pooled across test and generated scenes, excluding architectural elements. CKL is reported multiplied by 102. Pairwise layout relations. Our Pair-Rel metric compares the joint distributions of object-pair categories and relative geometry. For every ordered pair (i, j) of distinct furniture objects with valid bounding boxes, we form relation tuple rij = (ki, kj, dij, bij), where ki and kj are the object categories, dij is the direction of object relative to object i, and bij is distance bin. Both (i, j) and (j, i) contribute. To compute dij, we express the displacement between object centers in object is orientation frame. The axis with the larger displacement magnitude determines left, right, front, or back; coincident centers receive the label same. We measure distance as the minimum horizontal separation between the objects oriented bounding boxes, assigning zero to intersecting boxes. The distance bins are contact ( 0.05 m), near ((0.05, 0.5] m), mid ((0.5, 1.5] m), and far (> 1.5 m). We pool relation tuples across all scenes in each set and normalize their counts to obtain generated and ground-truth histograms Pgen and Pgt. Let = 2 (Pgen + Pgt). Pair-Rel is PairRel = 100 JSD(Pgen, Pgt) = 50 [DKL(PgenM ) + DKL(PgtM )] . (6) Lower values indicate closer agreement. Because object categories are included in each tuple, PairRel reflects both pair composition and relative geometry. Physical plausibility. OOBS is the fraction of generated scenes containing at least one object outside the room boundary. OOBO is the fraction of generated objects outside the room boundary. COL measures collisions among generated objects after connected-component grouping, orientation estimation, and object placement. NAV evaluates free-space navigability in the final scene. Opening clearance (OC) is the percentage of evaluated room-facing door and window clearance regions that do not intersect furniture mesh. Mean object count is reported alongside physical metrics to expose empty or unusually sparse generation. All metrics use the final scenes and evaluation protocol described in Sec. 4.1.

sections.content: Representation sanity checks. We conduct set of representation checks to verify that RoomTokens preserve object visibility, instance separation, and orientation before model evaluation. The processed data keeps 99.47% of furniture boxes visible, has 0.00% invalid tokens, only 0.92% sameclass color conflicts, and 1.13 direct orientation MAE, indicating little representation loss. RoomToken diagnostics. These metrics evaluate the RoomTokens representation and are not used to compare methods. Table 9 reports dataset-level statistics of the processed 3D-FRONT RoomToken representation before model training. Object coverage measures the fraction of furniture boxes that appear in at least one rasterized height slice. Invalid token counts semanticinstance-colorfacing triples that violate the representation rules. Theorem 1 (Four-color sufficiency for connected regions in single slice). Consider one height slice in which each object instance occupies set of grid cells connected through shared edges. For each semantic class k, connect two instances when their cells share grid edge. Then there exists an assignment of at most four colors such that every adjacent pair has different colors. Proof. The graph connecting cells that share an edge in single slice is planar. Remove cells belonging to other semantic classes and contract each instances connected cells into one vertex. Edge contraction and deletion preserve planarity, so the resulting instance-adjacency graph is planar. The four-color theorem therefore gives the required coloring (Appel and Haken, 1977; Robertson et al., 1997). We use this coloring principle to encode instance information with compact palette. In preprocessing, greedy coloring assigns each instance one consistent color across slices. The combined adjacency graph across slices need not be planar, and greedy coloring is not guaranteed to find four-color assignment. We choose three colors empirically: 99.08% of adjacent same-category, different-instance token pairs have different colors (App. C), and three colors yield lower COL and higher OC than four colors (Tab. 3). The null label denotes an inapplicable attribute and is not fourth instance color. CONDITIONING, INFERENCE, AND SCENE ASSEMBLY DETAILS Arch-mask conditioning. The conditioning tuple in Eq. (4) is written as κ = (r, a) in the main text to keep the denoising notation compact. Here is the room type and is the input arch mask. Cells with ai = 1 are clamped to their architectural labels during both forward masking and reverse denoising, while cells with ai = 0 are generated by the model. This lets MDIRT sample semantic, instance-color, and facing fields for furniture while preserving the supplied room geometry. Sampling. The three token fields are generated within one reverse diffusion process. Architectural tokens are fixed throughout; all unfixed cells initially have their semantic, instance-color, and facing fields masked. Each reverse step proceeds as follows: 1. Predict and update masked semantic labels according to the reverse schedule, retaining already revealed labels. 2. Recompute instance-color and facing predictions using the updated semantic state and shared denoiser features. 3. Keep both attributes masked if semantics remain masked. For revealed furniture semantics, reveal eligible attribute fields according to the schedule; for architecture/background semantics, assign null attributes. 4. Enforce compatible field values while preserving unresolved masks, and restore the fixed architectural tokens. For example, after semantic label becomes chair, instance color or facing may be revealed in that step or remain masked until later step. Such partially masked tokens are valid intermediate states. mask means that value is unknown; null means that an attribute is inapplicable. App. reports the denoising trajectory over 256 steps. The final grid preserves the supplied architectural tokens before grouping and asset placement. Token-to-object assembly. We group connected RoomTokens with the same semantic and instancecolor labels across height slices into object instances. Each instances tokens determine its category, horizontal center, and horizontal dimensions at grid resolution. The occupied height slices provide coarse vertical extent, while the body/front labels indicate orientation. MLP heads within MDIRT estimate continuous height and vertical offset from its denoising features. For each instance, we form 2D mask containing every grid cell where it appears in any height slice. We average the denoising features within this mask and feed the resulting vector to the heads. yaw head provides orientation when the body/front labels do not determine the direction. These predictions, together with the attributes obtained directly from the tokens, specify each objects category, position, dimensions, and orientation for asset retrieval and placement. Scene assembly for field-removal ablations. With RoomTokens, our instance colors allow us to generate object instances with spatial extent and orientation information. Our full model groups tokens by semantic and instance-color labels and uses the body/front cues to predict orientation. To ablate the removal of fields such as instance-color and facing, we follow SemLayoutDiff Sun et al. (2026) on how to handle instance identification and orientation. Without the instance color field, we use connected-component analysis to group connected tokens of the same semantic category into an object. In this case, adjacent same-category tokens are merged into the same instance. Without the facing field, we use an auxiliary instance-level MLP head to predict the yaw from pooled instance features. Note that the yaw is not fixed to zero. Asset retrieval and placement follow the same procedure for all of these variants. Asset retrieval. The final scene is instantiated by retrieving assets from 3D-FUTURE Fu et al. (2021b). For each object record, we first filter candidate assets by category, with fallback to compatible coarse labels when exact labels are unavailable. We convert the predicted object size (w, d, h) to 3D-FUTURE half-extents (w/2, h/2, d/2) and select the candidate with the smallest squared error in this 3D size space. The selected asset is scaled along each axis to match the estimated extents, rotated by the predicted yaw, translated to the recovered object position, and exported together with the reconstructed floor, wall, door, and window elements. The categoryand size-based retrieval and placement procedure follows SemLayoutDiff. We evaluate the resulting scenes directly, without subsequent clipping, optimization, or hand-designed correction. The reported zero OOB describes boundary compliance of these final scenes. 22 Effects of rotation and scaling. Even at fixed position, changing an objects yaw or size can make its bounding box extend past wall (OOB), cause collision (COL), or block passage (NAV). In Tab. 10, MDIRT placement gives zero OOB.
